You've put your finger right on the problem. Writers like Hines and Sillitoe aren't particularly great, but they appealed to a particular audience at the time they wrote, and so they were excessively lauded by the critics of that time. The whole gritty northern realism thing was a product of its time - the post-war period where grammar school boys were finally breaking the grip of the former establishment. Naturally, these homines novi would advance the cause of artists who provided the necessary cultural background music to their ascent. Your pleasure in reading "writers who came from [your] background" is understandable, as is the political and social desire to support these writers and promulgate them into the mainstream. The problem is that neither of them is a particularly good writer. Certainly there is the odd clever sentence or telling metaphor, but overall most writers of that school are not subtle or profound. You like these writers for the same reason you support your home town's soccer team: they may not be any good, but they're from where you're from. The key mark of a good writer is to be able to tell a story that people will read and will want to keep reading. People do not read "Kes" or "Loneliness..." unless they're forced to, because they are boring and not particularly well-written. And, in my experience, people loathe the kind of obvious sermonising that this school of writers so loves.

I'm not so sure that "appreciation" is totally subjective, in drama or in any other art. I suspect that in any area there are works that are very widely regarded as "good", not just by specialists but by non-specialists. People may be forced to read "Richard II" in school because their teacher says so, but out in the real world people quote the play all the time, watch it on TV (the recent BBC version seemed to be selling well in the bookshop I was in the other day), and spend time and money to watch it on stage. It's one thing for someone to say "Oh, I love Shakespeare", but it's quite another to actually spend the money. The fact that people will vote with their money suggests that it's not just the critics but ordinary people who enjoy Shakespeare. I'm not saying that popularity on its own, or critical acclaim on its own, is enough to guarantee that something is better than average, but I am saying that when both the market and the critics agree that something is good this is pretty suggestive of real merit.
